blocks.text: A function is a named block of code that you can run whenever you want, as many times as you want. Write the logic once, then use it everywhere by its name.

blocks.alt: Functions: define, call, parameters, return value

blocks.text: As programs grow, functions are what keep them from turning into an unreadable mess. They let you name a piece of work and reuse it without copying and pasting.
Functions are how you stop repeating yourself. Give a job a name, then call that name instead of writing the same code again and again.
Think of a function like a recipe. You write down the steps once, give the recipe a name, and then anyone can follow it any time just by naming it.
You hand the function some ingredients, called arguments, it does its work, and it can hand back a result, called the return value.
Defining and Calling
You define a function once with a name, then call it by that name to run it.

codes.python:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

greet("Riya")   # Hello, Riya
greet("Amit")   # Hello, Amit

blocks.text: Defining a function does not run it. It just teaches the computer the steps. Calling it, by writing its name with brackets, is what actually runs it.
A parameter is a value you hand into a function so it can work with different inputs each time. It makes one function useful for many cases.

codes.python:
def square(x):
    print(x * x)

square(3)   # 9
square(7)   # 49

blocks.text: The same function handles any number you give it. Without parameters, you would need a separate function for every value, which defeats the purpose.
Return Values
Printing shows a result on the screen. Returning hands the result back to the code that called the function, so it can be stored or used further.

codes.python:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(3, 4)   # total is now 7
print(total * 2)    # 14, we used the returned value

blocks.text: Printing and returning are different. A function that prints shows something and gives nothing back. A function that returns hands you a value to keep using. Most reusable functions return.
Functions can take several parameters, separated by commas. The order you pass values in matches the order of the parameters.
Here width takes the first value and height the second. Passing them in the wrong order would give a different meaning, so order matters.
Default Arguments
You can give a parameter a default value, so the caller may leave it out. This makes a function flexible without needing extra versions.

codes.python:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    print(greeting, name)

greet("Riya")          # Hello Riya
greet("Riya", "Hi")    # Hi Riya

blocks.text: When the caller supplies the value, it is used. When they do not, the default steps in. This is a clean way to handle common cases simply.
Sometimes a function needs to hand back several results. Many languages let you return them together.
Here the function returns two values at once, and the caller unpacks them into two variables. It keeps related results neatly together.
Why Functions Matter
Functions are not just convenient, they make your whole program better in several ways.

items: Reuse: write the logic once and call it from anywhere.
Readability: a good function name explains what a block of code does.
Testing: small functions are easy to check on their own.
Fixing bugs: fix it in one place instead of in ten copies.
Teamwork: people can use your function without reading its insides.

blocks.text: The best functions do exactly one thing and have a name that says what that thing is. If you need the word "and" to describe a function, it is probably doing too much.

codes.python:
# doing too much
def handle_user(): ...   # validates AND saves AND emails

# better: one job each
def validate_user(): ...
def save_user(): ...
def email_user(): ...

blocks.text: Small, single purpose functions are easier to name, test, and reuse. When a function grows large, look for a job you can split out.
A Word on Scope
Variables created inside a function usually live only inside that function. This is called scope, and it is a good thing.
It keeps each function self contained and stops it from accidentally changing variables that belong to other parts of the program.

codes.python:
def demo():
    x = 5      # x lives only inside demo
    print(x)

demo()
# print(x) here would fail, x does not exist outside

blocks.text: Functions can call other functions. This lets you build big behaviour out of small, simple pieces.
Building larger functions from smaller ones is the heart of clean programming. Each piece stays simple and easy to trust.
A Peek at Recursion
A function is even allowed to call itself. This is called recursion, and it shines on problems that naturally break into smaller copies of themselves.
It feels strange at first, but it is just a function using its own recipe on a smaller version of the problem.
Every recursion needs a base case, a simple situation where it stops calling itself and just returns an answer.
Without a base case, the function calls itself forever, exactly like a while loop with no exit. The base case is what makes recursion safe.
When writing a recursive function, write the base case first. Ask yourself: what is the smallest, simplest input, and what is the answer for it?
Recursion Example: Factorial
Factorial is the classic first recursion. The factorial of n is n times the factorial of n minus one, and the factorial of zero is one.
Each call solves a slightly smaller problem, until it reaches the base case and the answers multiply back up.
Fibonacci can also be written recursively, since each number is the sum of the two before it.
This version is elegant but slow for large n, because it recomputes the same values many times. It is a great example of clear code that is not always efficient code.
Loops vs Recursion
Many problems can be solved with either a loop or recursion. Neither is always better.

items: Loops are usually faster and use less memory.
Recursion is often shorter and clearer for problems that split into smaller copies, like trees.

blocks.text: As a beginner, use whichever reads more clearly to you. As you grow, you will learn when each one truly shines.
A function name should say what the function does, ideally starting with a verb. Good names make code read like a story.

items: Prefer verbs: calculate_total, is_prime, send_email.
Avoid vague names like do_stuff or process.
Match the name to what it returns, so is_prime returns true or false.

blocks.text: When you can read a series of function calls and understand the program without opening any of them, you have named them well.
Functions That Return Nothing
Not every function returns a value. Some just do an action, like printing or saving. That is completely fine.
A function that only acts and returns nothing is still useful. Use return when you need a value back, and skip it when you only need the action.

content.title: 10. Passing a List to a Function

blocks.text: Functions can take whole lists, not just single values. This lets one function work on a collection of data.
You hand the function a list, it loops over the items, and returns a single result. This is the shape of countless real functions.
A Worked Example: A Small Toolkit
Let us build a few small functions and use them together, the way real programs are organised.
Notice count_evens uses is_even. Small functions built on smaller functions is exactly how clean, real programs are put together.
Some languages let you write a tiny function without a name, right where you need it. In Python these are called lambda functions.

codes.python:
square = lambda x: x * x
print(square(5))     # 25

blocks.text: A lambda is just a short, one line function. You will not need it early, but it is handy when a function is so small that naming it feels heavy.
For anything beyond a tiny one line job, a normal named function is clearer. Use lambdas sparingly and only when they genuinely read better.

items: Printing a result when you actually needed to return it
Forgetting the base case in recursion, causing endless calls
Passing arguments in the wrong order
Expecting a variable made inside a function to exist outside it
Writing one giant function that does far too many jobs

blocks.text: When a function misbehaves, print its arguments at the top and its result before it returns. Seeing what goes in and what comes out reveals most bugs fast.
What is the difference between print and return?
print shows a value on the screen. return hands the value back to the calling code so it can be stored or used. They are not the same.
When should I make something a function?
When you do the same work in more than one place, or when a block of code deserves a clear name to explain it.
Is recursion better than a loop?
Not always. Loops are usually faster. Recursion is clearer for problems that break into smaller copies. Use whichever reads best for the problem.
Why can I not use a variable from inside a function outside it?
Because of scope. Variables made inside a function live only there, which keeps functions independent and safe.

items: Function: a named, reusable block of code.
Parameter: a named input a function accepts.
Argument: the actual value passed to a parameter.
Return value: the result a function hands back.
Scope: where a variable can be used.
Recursion: a function calling itself.
Base case: the stopping point of a recursion.
Write a function that returns the larger of two numbers.
Write a function that checks whether a number is even.
Write a function that returns the sum of a list.
Write a recursive function for factorial.
Write a recursive function for the Fibonacci series.
Break a small program into three well named functions.

blocks.text: Functions are how real programs stay organised and reusable. With input, variables, operators, conditions, loops, and functions mastered, you have the full toolkit to start real DSA.
